items.title: Use ERROR and RECONCILIATION as logical groups
items.statement: The team decided to categorize background events into ERROR and RECONCILIATION logical groups for clarity and simplicity.
items.quote: I agree with keeping the logical groups as ERROR and RECONCILIATION. Based on your explanation and the current 6 BackgroundEvent.Type values, that split seems appropriate.

items.title: Separate lanes for event consumption contexts
items.statement: Separating logical lanes based on when an event is allowed to be consumed (e.g., poll vs. unsubscribe) improves robustness over a single queue with filtering.
items.quote: I think it would be more robust to separate logical lanes based on when an event is allowed to be consumed, rather than continuing with the current model where all events are placed into a single queue and the caller drains everything and then filters afterward.

items.title: Current BackgroundEvent lacks consumption context
items.statement: The absence of consumption context in BackgroundEvent leads to fragile solutions like the skipAssignmentEvents flag.
items.quote: one issue that has been pointed out in several tickets is that a Background Event does not carry any information about when it is supposed to be consumed. The absence of that information is what leads us to introduce flags such as skipAssignmentEvents

items.title: Keep logical groups clear over broad abstractions
items.statement: The team prioritizes keeping logical groups (e.g., errors, callbacks) clear rather than introducing broad abstractions like ConsumptionPolicy.
items.quote: I agree with your point about encapsulating the logic in the background event handler, good point, but worth aiming for not obfuscating the logical groups (errors, callbacks)

items.title: Propose explicit processing mode for BackgroundEvent
items.statement: sanghyeok An proposed replacing the skipAssignmentEvents flag with an explicit internal processing mode (e.g., POLL or UNSUBSCRIBE).
items.quote: we could replace it with an internal consumer-only processing mode. For example: boolean processBackgroundEvents(BackgroundEventProcessingMode processingMode)

items.title: Metadata loss risk with majority controller failure
items.statement: Losing a majority of controllers can cause unrecoverable metadata loss, including stale ISR/ELR or missing leader epochs, leading to unclean leader elections or write truncation.
items.quote: losing a majority of controllers can result in metadata loss -- stale ISR/ELR or missing leader epochs could lead to unclean leader elections or write truncation

items.title: Recover from controller majority loss
items.statement: To resume operations after losing a majority of controllers, operators can override the voter set, but this may involve accepting data loss and risks stale ISR-based leader elections.
items.quote: operators facing permanent loss of 2 of 3 controllers still need some path to resume operations, even accepting data loss. After overriding the voter set

items.title: Recover from broker with highest log offset
items.statement: Recovering from a broker with the highest log end offset minimizes the risk of leadership epoch decreases for other brokers.
items.quote: If a broker holds the longest log, we "simply" copy its log onto a controller, and then add the voter set demotion records to the end of that copy

items.title: Scope of KIP-1347 voter set override
items.statement: Should KIP-1347's voter set override mechanism be limited to cases where all controllers are alive but unreachable, or include majority-loss recovery?
items.quote: Would you see KIP-1347's voter set override as a reasonable mechanism to resume cluster operations in this scenario, with the understanding that some metadata loss is unrecoverable? Or should this KIP explicitly scope itself to the "all controllers alive but unreachable" case

items.title: Multi-classloader SASL/OAUTHBEARER issue
items.statement: Using dynamically-loaded security providers in a multi-classloader environment causes SASL/OAUTHBEARER to fail for all but the first application in the JVM.
items.quote: this appears to be a pitfall of using dynamically-loaded security providers in a multi-classloader environment

items.title: Shared classloader for Kafka clients
items.statement: Moving Kafka client libraries to a shared parent classloader resolves the multi-classloader SASL/OAUTHBEARER issue.
items.quote: move kafka-client library(along with the libraries it depends on) out of application A and B and put the libraries in tomcat/lib/

items.title: JVM-wide security provider registry
items.statement: The JVM-wide security provider registry retains only the first provider registered under a given name, causing classloader conflicts.
items.quote: Security.addProvider keeps only the first provider registered under a given name

items.title: Remove KafkaConnect label
items.statement: The issue affects all Kafka client users, not just Kafka Connect, so the KafkaConnect label was removed.
items.quote: I'll remove the KafkaConnect label, as this affects all users of clients, and not Connect in any way particularly

items.title: Headers are mutable and expensive to deep-copy
items.statement: Kafka's Headers object is mutable, and performing a deep copy eagerly would be costly.
items.quote: The problem is, that `Headers` is a mutable object, and it would be expensive to make a deep-copy eagerly.

items.title: DLQ retains headers without issue
items.statement: Kafka Connect's built-in dead letter queue retains headers without problems because no downstream Kafka records are created by a sink record.
items.quote: Kafka Connect's built-in dead letter queue also has this problem but retaining headers there is no problem because there are no downstream Kafka records created by a sink record

items.title: Patch snapshots headers before deserialization
items.statement: The decision was made to patch snapshots of headers before the user deserializer sees them to prevent mutation issues.
items.quote: Patch snapshots headers before the user Deserializer sees them, both for the deserialization and processing error paths.

items.title: Headers mutation affects DLQ records
items.statement: Mutating headers in deserialization can make DLQ records unreplayable with the same SerDe.
items.quote: mutating Deserializer that strips its serde-internal marker, DLQ record then unreplayable on the same SerDe

items.title: Ignore null for named groups config
items.statement: The configuration will treat unset and empty named groups the same, ignoring null to maintain consistency with cipher suite handling.
items.quote: I decided to ignore the null case, the configuration is either set (and we call setNamedGroups) or empty (and we don't call setNamedGroups). This is the same behavior than ciphers.

items.title: Split PR scope for KIP-1376
items.statement: PR #22865 will focus on clients and brokers, with OAuth and Connect REST portions deferred to follow-up PRs under the same KIP.
items.quote: Yes that's an option.

items.title: JDK named groups behavior
items.statement: The JDK distinguishes between unset (uses defaults) and explicitly empty (disables) named groups arrays.
items.quote: the JDK distinguishes an unset value from an empty named-groups array. An unset value preserves the provider defaults, while an explicitly empty array means that no named groups are enabled.

items.title: TLS validation responsibility
items.statement: Named-group compatibility with TLS versions is left to the JVM and SSL provider, similar to cipher suites.
items.quote: does not attempt to validate named-group compatibility with the configured TLS version. I agree that this should remain the responsibility of the JVM and SSL provider, consistent with how cipher suites are handled.

items.statement: Documentation will be updated to align with Java 27 and use x25519_mlkem768 in examples.
items.quote: I’ll also align the documentation with Java 27 and use x25519_mlkem768 in the examples.

items.title: SCRAM between controllers not possible

items.title: Race condition cause
items.statement: The race condition occurs when an Acceptor queues a SocketChannel to a Processor that has already drained and terminated, leaving the channel unclosed.
items.quote: we ensure the _hand-off_ is fail-fast and the Acceptor never leaves a channel queued to a Processor that has already drained and terminated

items.title: Fix for race condition
items.statement: Make Processor#accept check shouldRun and return false during shutdown, forcing the Acceptor to close the SocketChannel.
items.quote: the Processor’s accept(...) path now checks shouldRun and returns false when the processor is shutting down; on a false return the Acceptor immediately closes the SocketChannel

items.title: Processor lifecycle check
items.statement: The if (!started.get) check in Processor#close handles the case of a processor that failed to start and should not be removed.
items.quote: I noticed the if (!started.get) check seems to handle the specific case of a processor that failed to start. I'm hesitant to remove it as it might have unintended side effects.

items.statement: FencedInstanceIdException in static membership consumers disables heartbeat but does not stop the thread, causing it to await indefinitely.
items.quote: for static membership consumer, got FencedInstanceIdException wouldn't stop the current heartbeatThread, but just disable the heartbeat and continue then await().

items.title: Fix approach for heartbeat thread issue
items.statement: The team considered two fixes: ensuring a single heartbeat thread runs or preventing new thread creation after FencedInstanceIdException.
items.quote: I think there are two fix way, one is to initialize only one heartbeatThread, and make sure it's running. While the other way is like my fix (easier), it won't create a new heartbeatThread after got FencedInstanceIdException.

items.quote: Hmm, after I added volatile, it still was blocked some times.

items.quote: I believe this is not only the bug in 2.8.X, but it's also in 3.X.X.

items.title: Heartbeat timer bug causes CPU spin
items.statement: A failed re-authentication leaves the heartbeat timer expired, causing the poll loop to spin due to `timeToNextHeartbeat()` returning 0.
items.quote: When re-auth fails, the heartbeat timer is left expired, so `timeToNextHeartbeat()` returns 0 and the poll loop spins.

items.title: Backoff must be respected in heartbeat logic
items.statement: The fix ensures backoff is respected by checking `canSendRequest()` before returning 0 in `maximumTimeToWait()` when `shouldHeartbeatNow()` is true.
items.quote: `maximumTimeToWait()` now checks `canSendRequest()` before returning 0 when `shouldHeartbeatNow()` is true, so the backoff is respected instead of busy-waiting.

items.title: Combining conditions can defeat backoff
items.statement: Folding `shouldHeartbeatNow` into the `pollTimer.isExpired()` condition would short-circuit and defeat the backoff fix.
items.quote: folding `shouldHeartbeatNow` back into the first condition would short-circuit and defeat the backoff fix.

items.title: Keep split condition form for backoff
items.statement: The team decided to keep the split form of `pollTimer.isExpired()` and `shouldHeartbeatNow` to preserve the backoff fix.
items.quote: I kept trunk's UNSUBSCRIBED guard but used the split form this fix introduces (`pollTimer.isExpired()` alone returns 0, then the `shouldHeartbeatNow` branch checks `canSendRequest` before returning 0).

items.statement: If MirrorInfo.TopicId validation fails in CreateTopic, the request fails with INVALID_REQUEST or TOPIC_ALREADY_EXISTS, but only the invalid topic fails in a batch.

items.title: Mirror state cache population
items.statement: The mirror partition cache in MirrorMetadataManager is populated by replaying __mirror_state partitions the broker leads and fetching state from remote coordinators for leadership changes.

items.title: NumPartitions field necessity
items.statement: The NumPartitions field in mirror requests is needed for the controller to create the destination topic if it doesn't exist, as the source topic's partition count may be unknown.
items.quote: The NumPartitions field is needed so the controller can create the destination topic if it does not already exist. When a topic is being mirrored for the first time, the destination cluster has no knowledge of the source topic's partition count, so the request must carry it.

items.title: HW and LSO are batch-aligned
items.statement: High watermark (HW) and Last Stable Offset (LSO) always align with batch boundaries due to replication and firstUnstableOffset() behavior.
items.quote: Since replication is at batch level, HW is always at batch boundary. Ditto for LSO since firstUnstableOffset() is at batch boundary.

items.title: Find MAX_TIMESTAMP within fetchable bound
items.statement: To find MAX_TIMESTAMP within a fetchable bound, use segment-level MAX_TIMESTAMP if within bounds, otherwise perform a binary search on the time index and scan batches up to the bound.
items.quote: If segment level MAX_TIMESTAMP is within the bound (e.g. HWM or Last Stable Offset), we can just use that. Otherwise, use the index on the segment containing the bound to find the MAX_TIMESTAMP.

items.title: Unregister a KRaft voter in static quorum
items.statement: To unregister a mistakenly configured voter in a static KRaft quorum, first remove it from controller.quorum.voters on all nodes before running the unregister command.
items.quote: Now, we need to remove the voter from controller.quorum.voters before unregistering it. Unregister a voter in a static KRaft quorum when the static voter set is mistakenly configured 1. Stop the voter who was mistakenly put in controller.quorum.voters 2. Run kafka-cluster unregister-controller 3. Ensure the stopped voter is not part of controller.quorum.voters on every Kafka node

items.title: Flush data-driven instead of transaction-boundary
items.statement: The team decided to make bundle flushing data-driven by using flush markers emitted by sources, rather than aligning with Kafka Streams transaction boundaries.

items.title: EOS and punctuation are incompatible
items.statement: Kafka Streams' EOS does not support punctuation (wall-clock or event-time) as they are side-effects not covered by EOS guarantees.
items.quote: punctuation in combination with EOS are tricky. EOS guarantees that you read some messaged, producer the corresponding output, and atomically commit the result records plus the advanced input topic offsets. Punctuations, wall-clock and event-time, don't really fit into this pattern.

items.title: Windows disk read errors may not propagate as I/O errors
items.statement: On Windows, disk read errors may result in non-I/O exceptions like EFAULT or WSAEINVAL due to memory mapping and driver behavior.
items.quote: the JDK writes the file to the socket from a memory mapping on both, and the write fails with EFAULT ("Bad address") on OpenBSD and WSAEINVAL ("An invalid argument was supplied") on Windows rather than with an I/O error.

items.quote: 3.9 compiles tests with `--release 8`, so `List.of`/`Set.of` became `Arrays.asList`, `Collections.singletonList` and `Collections.emptySet`.

items.title: 3.9 lacks MemoryRecords#slice
items.statement: The `MemoryRecords#slice` method does not exist in the 3.9 branch, necessitating alternative implementations for partial record handling.
items.quote: `MemoryRecords#slice` doesn't exist on 3.9, so `testRecordsEndingInPartialBatch` builds the partial `MemoryRecords` from a duplicate of the buffer with a lower limit.

items.title: FileRecords#slice throws IOException in 3.9
items.statement: In the 3.9 branch, `FileRecords#slice` throws an `IOException`, which must be declared in test methods.

items.title: Avoid prolonged hybrid mode
items.statement: Hybrid mode (ZK brokers with KRaft controller) should be minimized to the time required to restart brokers as KRaft.
items.quote: I would suggest only being in hybrid mode as long as it takes to restart the brokers as KRaft.

items.title: Dual-write mode is irreversible
items.statement: Once the migration to KRaft is finalized, there is no way to revert to ZooKeeper.
items.quote: Just note that once you finalize the migration, there is no going back.

items.title: Dual-write validation checks
items.statement: During dual-write mode, validate that client traffic is unaffected and broker health is stable.
items.quote: Generally, we like to see that client traffic is unaffected and broker health is stable.

items.title: Dual-write mode duration flexibility
items.statement: Clusters can remain in dual-write mode for hours, days, or weeks, depending on validation needs.
items.quote: You can stay in dual write mode for a few hours, days, or weeks.

items.title: Strict leader consistency check causes broker fencing
items.statement: The `hasConsistentLeader` check in `KafkaRaftClient.maybeTransition` is too strict and can incorrectly fence a broker during initial leader discovery.
items.quote: The condition if (!hasConsistentLeader(epoch, leaderId)) return; is too strict. For the first valid leader discovery (currentLeader empty, epoch matches), hasConsistentLeader returns false, causing the code path that leads to an IllegalStateException at line 2526, fencing the broker.

items.title: Long cleanup runs risk fencing
items.statement: Holding a transaction open past the timeout (e.g., 10s) causes the producer to be fenced, triggering repeated restores.
items.quote: a cleanup run of 14 to 18 seconds held the transaction open past the 10 second transaction timeout, the producer got fenced

items.title: Avoid ARCHIVING transition on persister failure
items.statement: The team decided to avoid transitioning records directly to ARCHIVING when the persister fails after retries to prevent stalling the in-flight records queue.
items.quote: This was deliberately avoided as a persister fail => a 5 time call to persister with exponential backoff failed. Now with DLQ again, the first step is ARCHIVING which requires a persister write. This too has good chance of failing (same partition key, so same broker). Hence the decision was taken to not stall the in-flight records queue over this.

items.title: Persister failure risks ARCHIVING failure

items.quote: ARCHIVING which requires a persister write. This too has good chance of failing (same partition key, so same broker).

items.title: ByteBuffer support rationale
items.statement: Supporting ByteBuffer as a value allows users to manage pooled/reused buffers more efficiently by allocating before send and releasing after, since data is copied to the accumulator immediately.
items.quote: There appears to be more sense in explicit support for ByteBuffer as a value so that user code can allocate it before calling producer.send and release after that since it's guaranteed that the contents have been copied to producer's accumulator by then

items.title: Serializer property constraint
items.statement: The mandatory 'value.serializer' property complicates ByteBuffer support because it is checked at KafkaProducer construction time, before any value is present.
items.quote: The only huccup here is that "value.serializer" property is mandatory and its presence is checked at KafkaProducer's contstruction time when there's no value present yet

items.title: Serializer workaround for ByteBuffer
items.statement: One workaround is to keep the value serializer mandatory but ignore it if the value is a ByteBuffer, as its contents can be copied without serialization.
items.quote: The other option is to keep value serializer mandatory like now but ignore it if the value is a ByteBuffer whose contents can be copied without any serializers

items.title: Callback-initiated send may deadlock
items.statement: A callback-initiated send can block the producer IO thread if buffer space is insufficient due to the original batch's buffer not being released until the callback returns.
items.quote: with memory for only one batch, a successful callback for A cannot enqueue B because A's buffer is released only after the callback returns.

items.title: Prep metadata before callback send
items.statement: Applications can avoid metadata-related recursion by calling producer.partitionsFor() to prepare metadata before sending in a callback.
items.quote: An alternative easier solution is for the application to call producer.partitionsFor() to prep the metadata before calling send() in the callback.

items.title: PR proposed for zero wait budget on IO thread
items.statement: The proposed solution sets maxWaitMs to 0 for doSend() when invoked on the producer's IO thread to prevent blocking, while retaining configured wait budgets for application threads.
items.quote: The proposed change gives doSend() a zero metadata/buffer wait budget only when invoked on that producer's I/O thread.

items.title: Unbounded recursion risk with zero wait
items.statement: Setting maxWaitMs to 0 when doSend() is called from the IO thread may cause unbounded synchronous recursion if metadata is not ready.
items.quote: If the metadata is not ready, this can lead to unbounded synchronous recursion on the Sender thread

items.title: Bug affects multiple Kafka client and JDK versions
items.statement: The IllegalMonitorStateException in KafkaProducer.waitOnMetadata has been observed across Kafka client versions 2.5.0, 2.5.1, 2.6.0, 2.7.0, and 3.1.0, as well as JDK versions 13, 14, 17, and Amazon Corretto 17.
items.quote: We have observed this bug on kafka client 2.5.0, 2.6.0 with kafka 2.0 and kafka 2.6.0 (openjdk-13, openjdk-14).

items.title: Restart application as workaround
items.statement: The only known workaround for the IllegalMonitorStateException is to restart the application, as creating a new producer does not resolve the issue.
items.quote: all we can do is restart application. We tried to work around the bug by creating a new producer - this didn't work.

items.title: Test with JDK 17 to confirm issue
items.statement: The team decided to test with JDK 17 to determine if the issue persists, as JDK 13 and 14 are out of support.
items.quote: The most helpful thing would be to test with JDK 17. If the problem still happens with that, that would be valuable information.

items.title: Bug occurs despite synchronized block
items.statement: The IllegalMonitorStateException is thrown even though the obj.wait() call is within a synchronized(obj) block, suggesting a potential OpenJDK issue.
items.quote: The IllegalMonitorStateException is thrown when the obj.wait() call is not within a synchronized(obj) block. But here it is within a synchronized block

items.title: Bug affects multiple producer instances
items.statement: The issue has been observed in multiple distinct producer instances within the same process, indicating it is not isolated to a single instance.
items.quote: We are running multiple distinct producer instances within the same process and several hit the issue.

items.title: Store corruption linked to broker patches

items.title: Theory on store corruption cause
items.statement: Store corruption may occur when a transient null committed offset and an EOS state wipe coincide during a broker patch.
items.quote: Two independent consequences of a broker patch have to land on the same task in the same window — either alone is survivable, but together they silently empty a store.
